mcqs.question: A view has only a leading constraint and a top constraint, with no width, height, trailing, or bottom constraint, and no intrinsic content size. What happens?
options: The view is centered automatically in its superview
Auto Layout throws a compile-time error requiring at least four constraints per view
The view's position and size are ambiguous, since the equations don't fully determine its frame
The view defaults to filling its superview's entire remaining space
mcqs.explanation: With only two constraints and no intrinsic size, the system of equations is under-determined — there's no unique solution for the view's frame, so Auto Layout is left to pick an unspecified one, which is the definition of an ambiguous layout. There's no compile-time constraint-count requirement, and no automatic centering or fill-remaining-space default.

mcqs.question: A view has a required (priority 1000) width constraint of 200pt and a lower-priority (750) constraint that would size it to 150pt. What does Auto Layout do?
options: It averages the two constraints, sizing the view to 175pt
It satisfies the required constraint and effectively drops the lower-priority one where they conflict, rendering the view at 200pt
It throws a runtime crash since the constraints are contradictory
It satisfies whichever constraint was added to the view first
mcqs.explanation: Required (1000) constraints must be satisfied; lower-priority constraints are broken when they conflict with a required one, rather than averaged or resolved by insertion order. A genuine conflict between two required constraints, not one required and one optional, is what triggers a runtime 'unable to satisfy constraints' warning.

mcqs.question: You need a row of views where one subview can be hidden and shown dynamically, with the rest automatically re-flowing to fill or make space. What's the simplest tool?
options: UIStackView, since toggling a subview's isHidden triggers automatic re-layout of its siblings
Raw NSLayoutConstraint, manually deactivating and reactivating constraints on show/hide
A fixed-frame layout, recalculating positions manually whenever visibility changes
Auto Layout cannot handle dynamic show/hide without a full layout rewrite
mcqs.explanation: UIStackView specifically handles the show/hide case well — setting isHidden on a subview automatically removes it from the layout flow and re-positions siblings, which raw constraints require manual constraint activation bookkeeping to replicate.

mcqs.question: Why is designing a layout against size classes more future-proof than designing against a specific device's pixel dimensions?
options: Size classes are guaranteed to never change, ever, across any future device
Pixel-based layouts are actually faster to render than size-class-based layouts
Size classes only apply to iPad, so this only matters for tablet layouts
The next iPhone's exact pixel width is unknown at build time, but its size class in portrait (compact-width/regular-height) is highly likely to stay the same as current models
mcqs.explanation: Size classes are a coarser, more stable abstraction than exact dimensions — new iPhone models keep shipping in the same compact-width/regular-height portrait class even as their exact pixel dimensions change, so code branching on size class survives new hardware that code branching on a specific pixel width would not. Size classes apply to iPhone as well as iPad, and neither approach inherently affects render speed.

mcqs.question: A view visibly jumps to a different position between layout passes with no code change, and the console shows no explicit crash. What's the most likely cause?
options: A memory leak in the view's superview is corrupting its frame
The view's layer has an animation that never completes
The view is ambiguously constrained, so Auto Layout is picking a technically-valid but unspecified frame each time it resolves
The device's screen refresh rate is causing the visual glitch
mcqs.explanation: An ambiguous layout has more than one mathematically valid solution, and Auto Layout doesn't guarantee picking the same one every pass — that inconsistency is exactly what produces an unexplained visual jump with no explicit crash. Xcode's view debugger and console warnings can confirm ambiguity directly.

mcqs.question: A layout computes a view's width as UIScreen.main.bounds.width / 2 - 40 and sets it as a fixed constant. What's the risk?
options: This is the recommended pattern for all Auto Layout width constraints
It reintroduces device-specific brittleness — the layout breaks or looks wrong on any device size the hardcoded math wasn't tuned for, including future devices
The risk is purely stylistic; functionally it behaves identically to a percentage-based multiplier constraint
This pattern only causes issues on iPad, never on iPhone
mcqs.explanation: Hardcoding a pixel calculation from a specific screen width defeats the purpose of Auto Layout's relative, solver-based model — it silently breaks on any device the math wasn't tuned for, unlike a multiplier-based relative constraint or a size-class-gated adjustment, which adapt automatically. The risk is functional, not just stylistic, and applies to any device size, not only iPad.
